passages.original: sed in uto magnitudinem suæ artis ostendit, ex luto plasmatum corrigens hominem, ipse ex virgine novi decoris homo procedens; modum quidem genituræ permutans, per oinnia vero ad nos absque peccato non diffugiendam similitudinem indicans, » Ex eadem synodo testimonium sancti Ambrosii : « Sileant igitur inanes de sermonibus quæstiones, quoniam regnum Dei, sicut scriptum est, non in persuasione humani verbi est, sed in ostensione virtutis ( 1 Cor. II. 4) : Servemus differentiam divinitatis et carnis : unus in utroque loquitur Dci Filius, quia in eodem utraque natura est; idem loquitur, sed non uno semper loquitur modo. Intende in eo, nunc quidem gloriam Dei, nunc vero hominis passiones : quia sicut Deus docet divina, quia Verbum est;
passages.english: but in clay he showed the greatness of his art, setting right the man formed from clay, he himself coming forth from a virgin as a man of new beauty; changing indeed the manner of birth, but showing in all things a likeness to us, without sin, that is not to be shunned." From the same synod, the testimony of Saint Ambrose: "Let empty questions about words therefore be silent, since the kingdom of God, as it is written, is not in the persuasion of human speech, but in the demonstration of power (1 Cor. 2:4). Let us keep the distinction between the divinity and the flesh: the one Son of God speaks in both, because both natures are in the same [one]; the same [one] speaks, but he does not always speak in one manner. Observe in him now the glory of God, now the sufferings of man: for as God he teaches divine things, because he is the Word;
passages.notes: 'in uto' is read as 'in luto' (in clay), continuing the quotation from Theophilus begun in the preceding context; 'oinnia' read as 'omnia', 'Dci' as 'Dei'. The phrase 'non diffugiendam similitudinem' is rendered literally ('a likeness not to be shunned'); the sense is somewhat uncertain.

passages.original: die mibi : nonne manifesta est differentia naturarum ? Quod enim cœpit, ct profecit ct ad perfectionem pervenit, caro est : quod vero semper est, et secundum naturam ct substantiam perfectissimum, Deus esi. Quia igitur, ,'estin entes ut Arius, dicunt de Domino crucifixo, quia Incitas ejus non secundum naturam et substantiam perfectis ima est, scd pcr donum vcl mercedem honorem percepit a Patre : quippe quæ vertibilis sit altune mutabilis;
passages.english: Tell me: is not the difference of the natures evident? For what began, and advanced, and came to perfection, is flesh; but what always is, and is most perfect according to nature and substance, is God. Since, therefore, those who are mad like Arius say of the crucified Lord that his deity is not most perfect according to nature and substance, but that it received honour from the Father by gift or reward, seeing that it is changeable, or rather mutable;
passages.notes: Many scanning errors corrected silently (mibi = mihi, ct = et, esi = est, scd = sed, pcr = per, vcl = vel, perfectis ima = perfectissima). ",'estin entes" is read as "insanientes" ("being mad"); this is uncertain. "Incitas" is read as "Deitas" ("deity"), which agrees with "Deitatem" in the following context. "altune" is read as "atque" or "aut" ("or rather"). The sentence is incomplete and continues in the following text with "the most holy Gregory objected against [this]…".

passages.original: Verum illud affirmo, quia hic necesse est a me exigi causam : etenim et omnes sancti Patres, et vos ipsi naturae divinitatis connu- It e: atis carnem : ex duabus enim naturis dicitis Christum. Quod si divinitati non connumeratur humanitas, non solum in cis esse, sed ct ex ipsis esse, dicere non debemus. Non igitur ex duabus cst. Sed et Ambrosius male|, secundumvos, inquit: « Unus in utroque loquitur Dei Filius, quia in eo utraque natura est; » et Gregorius dicens : c Duæ naturæ Deus et homo, quia et anima et corpus ; » et Cyrillus dicens : < Duarum enim naturarum unitio facta est ;
passages.english: But I affirm this, because here it is necessary that the reason be demanded of me: for both all the holy Fathers and you yourselves count the flesh together with the nature of the divinity: for you say that Christ is from two natures. But if the humanity is not counted together with the divinity, we ought not to say that he not only is in them, but also is from them. Therefore he is not from two. But Ambrose too, according to you, speaks wrongly when he says: "The one Son of God speaks in both, because both natures are in him"; and Gregory, saying: "Two natures, God and man, as also soul and body"; and Cyril, saying: "For a union of two natures has taken place;
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected silently: 'connu- It e: atis' read as 'connumeratis', 'cis' as 'eis', 'ct' as 'et', 'cst' as 'est', 'male|' as 'male'. The argument is compressed and the logic of the first sentences is somewhat obscure; 'naturae divinitatis' is taken as dative ('with the nature of the divinity').
